conventions.statement: A positive integer is prime exactly when it has two distinct positive divisors.
A positive integer is composite when it has more than two distinct positive divisors.
The positive integer 1 has one positive divisor and is neither prime nor composite.
A divisor card is complete and contains no duplicate positive divisors.

capabilities.action: Classify a positive integer from a COMPLETE positive-divisor card by the defining divisor-count criterion.
capabilities.success_criterion: Choose prime/composite/neither from the count; rule out the oddness heuristic and reverse-select a card satisfying prime.

microtopics.title: Discriminate prime, composite and one by the exact divisor-count condition
microtopics.badge_reason: One classifying act from a supplied complete factor card.
entry_assumptions: Understand positive divisibility and a list of distinct divisors.
The displayed list is complete and excludes unseen factors.
Categories are prime, composite, or neither.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Retrieve the exact count-of-distinct-divisors criterion, avoiding the superficial 'odd implies prime' heuristic.

teaching_path.action: Recognize a COMPLETE positive-divisor card and count its DISTINCT entries.
teaching_path.why_valid: Definition uses the full set of distinct positive divisors, not repeated multiplication factors.

teaching_path.action: Prime means EXACTLY TWO distinct positive divisors; composite means MORE than TWO; 1 has only ONE and is neither.
teaching_path.why_valid: The three cases partition positive integers by the defining conditions.

teaching_path.action: Work a separate example: 13 has the complete list {1,13}, thus has two distinct positive divisors and is prime.
teaching_path.why_valid: 13 has no other positive divisors; exactly two meets the prime criterion.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: An odd positive integer must be prime.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A learner calls 9 prime solely because it is odd, even though the complete positive-divisor card is {1,3,9}. Which exact count disproves the claim?
misconceptions.repair: Oddness is not the defining criterion. Three distinct positive divisors mean 9 is composite.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If a number is not composite, it must be prime, including 1.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: The complete positive-divisor list for 1 is {1}. Does one divisor meet exactly two?
misconceptions.repair: One is neither prime nor composite; prime requires exactly two distinct positive divisors.

exit_task.prompt: Independent exit: the complete positive-divisor card for 22 is {1,2,11,22}. Classify 22 as prime, composite or neither and cite the exact count.

reasoning: The four numbers 1,2,11,22 are four distinct positive divisors.
Four is greater than two, which is the composite criterion.
answer.check: 2×11=22 gives a nontrivial factor pair; the complete divisor card agrees.

microtopics.research_contribution: Original D1 defining-category task with an odd-composite near neighbour, exclusion of 1 and reversed category-to-card transfer; academic review pending.

construction_units.decision: Retrieve and use exact cardinality of complete positive-divisor set.

independent_checks.statement: Verify the count against a nontrivial factor pair or the singleton set.

compact_anchor.prompt: What is the exact criterion for PRIME rather than COMPOSITE or NEITHER?
compact_anchor.result: Prime exactly two distinct positive divisors; composite more than two; 1 with one divisor neither.

predict.prompt: A classmate claims 9 is prime because it is odd. Its complete distinct positive-divisor card is {1,3,9}. Before opening the correction, decide whether oddness proves prime and why.
predict.defensible_answer: No. Three distinct positive divisors make 9 composite, despite being odd.

attempt.produces: An independently written diagnosis of the oddness claim, corrected category and a new boundary decision.

rubric.criterion: Reject oddness as the classification criterion.
Use the definition to identify the correct class.
rubric.evidence_of: Three distinct divisors, more than two, composite.

accepted: 9 is composite because 1,3,9 are three distinct positive divisors. Being odd does not imply prime.
rejected: Odd numbers are prime, so 9 is prime.

task.prompt: A learner writes: '9 is prime because it is odd.' The complete positive-divisor set is {1,3,9}. Explain whether this criterion works, and independently name the correct category before revealing the reconstruction.
givens: Prime requires exactly two distinct positive divisors.
Composite requires more than two distinct positive divisors.

route.ask: Does the defining condition test oddness, or the exact positive-divisor count?
route.why_this_ask: Separates near-neighbour familiarity from the criterion.

route.ask: Count distinct divisors on 9's complete card. Does that match the prime requirement?
route.why_this_ask: Uses a falsifying case instead of announcing the answer.

route.ask: Which category contains positive integers with more than two positive divisors?

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: A correct 13 card is explained in Core1A; Core1B starts from a classmate's incorrect oddness shortcut for 9 and asks the learner to falsify it using a complete factor list.

boundary_test.prompt: Changed case: the positive integer 1 has complete positive-divisor list {1}. Choose prime, composite or neither using the exact count; commit your answer before checking.
boundary_test.answer: Neither. One has only one distinct positive divisor and meets neither the exactly-two nor the greater-than-two criterion.
boundary_test.confirms: The repaired concept works on the excluded singleton boundary, not only on odd composite 9.

relations.expression: A prime has exactly two distinct positive divisors; a composite has more than two; 1 has exactly one.
relations.meaning: Category depends on the count in a complete distinct-positive-divisor set, not oddness.

symbols.meaning: Count of distinct positive divisors of n

conditions: The provided divisor card is complete and distinct

limits: An odd number may be composite, as 9 is.
One is neither prime nor composite.

questions.stem: Worked teaching example: from an origin, a walker travels three grid units west and one north. Write a signed (x,y) displacement and check by translating back.
conditions: Map origin is fixed; east is positive x and north is positive y.
Horizontal x is written first, vertical y second.
Original authored TEST; not an official examination item.

reasoning: Three west means horizontal x is −3.
One north means vertical y is +1.
With x first, the pair is (−3,+1).
The reverse translation gives three west and one north.

reasoning_route.action: Translate three west and one north into (−3,+1).
reasoning_route.why_valid: Negative x is west and positive y is north; order is x then y.

answer.check: Translate (−3,+1) back to three west, one north.

questions.failure_signal: A signed coordinate encodes direction, not just a positive length; reverse the pair into words.

independent_check.statement: Translate (−3,+1) back to three west, one north.

questions.stem: A surveyor starts at the origin of an east-positive/north-positive square grid. She records a displacement of 4 grid units EAST and 2 grid units SOUTH. Write the displacement as a signed ordered pair (x,y), with horizontal first. Explain the sign of its second entry.
conditions: Map origin is fixed; east is positive x and north is positive y.
Horizontal x is written first, vertical y second.
Original authored TEST; not an official examination item.

answer.summary: (4,−2); y is negative because south is opposite positive north.
reasoning: Four units east gives horizontal x=+4.
Two units south gives vertical y=−2 because north is positive.

reasoning_route.action: Identify four east as the horizontal component and two south as the vertical component.
reasoning_route.why_valid: This map declares horizontal east-west as x and vertical north-south as y.
reasoning_route.output: x component comes from east; y component comes from south.

reasoning_route.action: Assign the correct signs and order the components as (4,−2).
reasoning_route.why_valid: East is positive x, south opposes positive north and is negative y, and x precedes y.

reasoning_route.action: Read (4,−2) backward as four east and two south.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The reverse meaning equals both given movements, so no direction or magnitude was lost.

answer.check: Read (4,−2) as four east and two south; both givens match.

scaffolds.text: Which part of the description belongs to the first, horizontal entry, and which to the second, vertical entry? Do not sign either for the learner.
Compare each named movement to the positive direction of its own axis. A magnitude alone does not determine the sign.
After recording your attempt, review x-before-y and translate both signs back to directions to see whether the route is preserved.

questions.stem: A second map report gives the signed displacement (−3,+5) from the origin using the SAME east-positive/north-positive grid convention. This time write a sentence describing the direction and magnitude of each movement, rather than writing another pair. Explain how encoding your sentence back checks it.
conditions: Map origin is fixed; east is positive x and north is positive y.
Horizontal x is written first, vertical y second.
Original authored TEST; not an official examination item.

answer.summary: Three units west and five units north.
reasoning: The first entry −3 is horizontal and means three west.
The second entry +5 is vertical and means five north.
The route is three grid units west and five grid units north.

reasoning_route.action: Read the first entry of (−3,+5) as horizontal and second as vertical.
reasoning_route.why_valid: By definition ordered pairs store x then y.

reasoning_route.action: Translate the signed entries to three west and five north.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Negative x points west, positive y points north under the fixed map convention.

reasoning_route.action: Encode the spoken route to recover (−3,+5).
reasoning_route.why_valid: The reverse map reproduces the supplied signed ordered pair exactly.

answer.check: Reverse-encode the words to (−3,+5), exactly the supplied pair.
